children: Economists have brought forward rate-hike expectations as higher crude prices, rising inflation and global bond yields limit the RBI’s room to hold rates

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) could raise the repo rate by 25 basis points (bps) in October, bringing forward the start of its rate-hike cycle as higher crude oil prices, rising inflation and elevated global bond yields put pressure on the central bank to tighten monetary policy.

The RBI’s Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) is scheduled to meet from 5-7 October to decide on the benchmark policy rate. Economists had earlier expected the rate-hike cycle to begin in December, but the recent deterioration in inflation and global financial conditions has led some forecasters to bring forward their expectations.

Bank of America (BofA) has revised its forecast and now expects a 25 bps repo rate increase at the October meeting, compared with its earlier call for a December hike. The brokerage said rising energy prices, food inflation and broader inflationary pressures could prompt the RBI to begin withdrawing monetary support after nearly two years of easing.

The State Bank of India (SBI) has also favoured an early policy response, citing geopolitical tensions, risks from higher crude oil prices and a reassessment of global risks. Its report said it would be prudent for the RBI to act pre-emptively rather than wait for these risks to intensify.

Domestic inflation has added to the pressure. Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation rose to 4.82 per cent in August from 4.45 per cent in July. Food inflation could face further risks if a strong El Niño and below-normal rainfall in October affect rabi crop yields. Higher crude prices and global bond yields have also narrowed the RBI’s room to keep interest rates unchanged.
BNP Paribas India said the country’s macroeconomic outlook had weakened in recent weeks as Brent crude moved above USD 100 a barrel and the US 10-year Treasury yield approached 5 per cent.

Despite the possibility of an October hike, economists do not expect the RBI to embark on an aggressive tightening cycle. Analysts at global brokerage Nomura expect cumulative rate increases of 25-50 bps in the current cycle and estimate an 80 per cent probability of a limited tightening cycle, rather than an increase of more than 75 bps.
A basis point is one-hundredth of a percentage point. A 25 bps increase, therefore, would raise the repo rate by 0.25 percentage point.
